items.item: Separating the decision point from the enforcement point is what lets many different data-access surfaces (a warehouse, a query engine, an API) share one policy engine and one audited policy, instead of each implementing its own access logic.

items.item: OPA and Cedar both evaluate the same shape of question (is this principal allowed this action on this resource) but Cedar's language is purpose-built for authorization while Rego is a general-purpose policy language also used for non-authorization checks.

at.step: Reveal: what the policy engines actually hand back

items.item: SAML and OIDC both authenticate a person once at the IdP, but SCIM is a separate, independent protocol for keeping the downstream account and group records themselves in sync — authentication and provisioning are two different problems solved by different protocols.

at.step: Reveal: provisioning keeps accounts and groups in sync

items.item: Offboarding appears automatic only because SCIM provisioning is wired to the IdP's own group membership; a downstream system not wired to SCIM would keep a removed employee's access until someone manually revokes it.

at.step: Reveal: offboarding in one place, everywhere at once

items.item: A periodic access review exists because a policy evaluated correctly every time still grants access the policy's own rule says is correct, even when the underlying reason for that grant (a finished project, a changed role) no longer holds; the review catches drift in intent, not errors in evaluation.

at.step: Reveal: periodic access reviews catch what policy never will
